running-python-code.label: Running Python Code
running-python-code.summary: Use the editor–Run–output cycle, follow top-to-bottom execution, and improve a program by editing and running it again.

sketch1.title: Python runs the current program top to bottom

sc_runner_parts.title: Follow the run cycle
sc_runner_parts.prompt: Which sequence describes the normal way to test Python code in ZoeSkoul?
sc_runner_parts.hint: Code is written before it can be executed and observed.

help.concept: The basic cycle is: edit the program, run the current code, then inspect what the run produced.
help.hint_1: The output panel shows results; it is not where source code is written.

options.a: Write or edit code → click Run → inspect the output
options.b: Inspect the output → click Run → write the program
options.c: Type the program into the output panel → click Run
options.d: Click Run and let Python invent the program automatically

sc_source_vs_output.title: Know where to make a change
sc_source_vs_output.prompt: You ran a program and want to change its second line. Where should you make that change?
sc_source_vs_output.hint: The output panel shows results from a run.

help.concept: Source code is edited in the code editor. The output panel shows the result produced when the program runs.
help.hint_1: Do not edit the displayed output and expect the program to change.
help.hint_2: Change the source code in the editor, then run it again.

mc_run_cycle_facts.title: Understand edit and rerun
mc_run_cycle_facts.prompt: Which statements about the edit–Run–output cycle are true? Choose all correct answers.
mc_run_cycle_facts.hint: Think about when code changes take effect in the displayed result.

help.concept: Editing changes the source program. Running executes the current program and produces a new result that you can compare with the previous one.
help.hint_1: A code edit is not the same action as executing the code.
help.hint_2: Running again after an edit is how you observe the changed behavior.

options.a: Run executes the current code in the editor.
options.b: Editing source code automatically rewrites the previous output without another run.
options.c: After editing, running again lets you observe the new result.
options.d: The output panel is the main place to type Python source code.

dr_run_steps.title: Order one test cycle
dr_run_steps.prompt: Arrange the actions for one useful code-testing cycle.
dr_run_steps.hint: Make a change before executing it.

help.concept: A useful cycle is edit → run → inspect. You use what you observe to decide whether another edit is needed.
help.hint_1: Execution comes after the code change.
help.hint_2: Inspection comes after the run produces a result.

dr_program_flow.title: Follow top-to-bottom execution
dr_program_flow.prompt: This program contains three output statements in this order: `First`, `Second`, `Third`. Arrange the resulting output.
dr_program_flow.hint: For these simple statements, Python executes from the first line downward.

help.concept: Python normally executes simple statements from top to bottom, so their visible results appear in the same sequence.
help.hint_1: Start with the result produced by the first code line.
help.hint_2: Keep the same order as the source statements.

fb_after_edit_output.title: Predict the next run
fb_after_edit_output.prompt: A program previously printed `Draft`. You change its only line to `print("Ready")` and click Run again. What should the new output contain?
fb_after_edit_output.hint: The new run uses the current code.

help.concept: When you run after an edit, Python executes the edited program, so the new output reflects the new source code.
help.hint_1: Ignore what the previous run displayed.
help.hint_2: Use the text in the edited statement.

ci_run_first_edit.title: Make a change and run it
ci_run_first_edit.prompt:
The starter program prints `Draft`. Change the program so the next run prints exactly:

`Ready`
ci_run_first_edit.hint: Edit the string in the existing output statement.

help.concept: The editor contains the source program. After changing the source, run the program again to see the new result.

0.message: Keep one print call and make it display exactly Ready.

ci_top_to_bottom_order.title: Put output statements in execution order
ci_top_to_bottom_order.prompt:
Reorder the starter program so its output is exactly:

`First`
`Second`
`Third`
ci_top_to_bottom_order.hint: The first source line runs before the lines below it.

help.concept: For this straight-line program, Python executes each statement from top to bottom.
help.hint_1: Move the line that prints `First` to the top.
help.hint_2: The source order should match the required output order.

0.message: Place the three print calls in First, Second, Third order.

ci_edit_rerun_preserve.title: Change one result and preserve the rest
ci_edit_rerun_preserve.prompt:
The starter program already prints two lines. Change only what is necessary so the next run prints exactly:

`Status`
`Version 2`
ci_edit_rerun_preserve.hint: The first line is already correct.

help.concept: A focused edit changes the part that needs improvement while preserving code that already produces the correct result.
help.hint_2: Edit the text in the second statement, then run again.

0.message: Preserve Status on the first line and change only the second result to Version 2.

ci_practice_insert_middle_line.title: Insert a missing middle output
ci_practice_insert_middle_line.prompt:
Add one line between the existing statements so the program prints:

`Start`
`Middle`
`End`
ci_practice_insert_middle_line.hint: Insert the new statement between the two existing statements.

help.concept: In straight-line code, the position of a statement determines when its output appears.
help.hint_1: Do not remove the correct first or last line.
help.hint_2: Add the statement that produces `Middle` between them.

0.message: Insert Middle between the existing Start and End output statements.

ci_practice_reorder_output.title: Reorder a four-line program
ci_practice_reorder_output.prompt:
Reorder the existing statements so the program prints exactly:

`North`
`East`
`South`
`West`
ci_practice_reorder_output.hint: Match source order to required output order.

help.concept: With simple sequential statements, output order follows the top-to-bottom order of the code.
help.hint_1: You do not need new statements.
help.hint_2: Move each existing line into the same order as the target output.

0.message: Reorder the four existing print calls to North, East, South, West.

ci_practice_change_middle.title: Edit only the middle line
ci_practice_change_middle.prompt:
Change only the middle output so the program prints:

`Red`
`Gold`
`Green`
ci_practice_change_middle.hint: The first and third statements are already correct.

help.concept: A targeted edit preserves correct behavior while changing only the part required by the new goal.
help.hint_1: Do not rewrite the whole program.
help.hint_2: Change `Blue` to `Gold` in the middle statement.

0.message: Preserve Red and Green and change only the middle result to Gold.

ci_practice_extend_program.title: Extend a working program
ci_practice_extend_program.prompt:
The first two lines are already correct. Add two more statements so the complete output is:

`Step 1`
`Step 2`
`Step 3`
`Step 4`
ci_practice_extend_program.hint: Keep the working lines and continue below them.

help.concept: You can extend a straight-line program by adding new statements after the existing ones.
help.hint_2: Append statements for `Step 3` and `Step 4` in that order.

0.message: Keep the first two steps and extend the program through Step 4 in order.

sketch_run_cycle.title: From code editor to output
sketch_run_cycle.bodyMarkdown:
When you work on a Python exercise in ZoeSkoul, three parts have different jobs:

1. **Code editor** — where you write or change the program
2. **Run** — executes the current program
3. **Output panel** — shows what that run produced

Think of the workflow as:

```text
edit code → Run → inspect result
```

Suppose the editor contains:

```python
print("Draft")
```

After you run it, the output shows:

```text
Draft
```

Now change the source code to:

```python
print("Ready")
```

The program has changed in the editor. Run it again to observe the result of the new version.

The important distinction is:

- **source code** is what you control
- **output** is evidence of what the last run did

You will use this edit–Run–inspect cycle throughout the course.

sketch_print_and_strings.title: Python runs the current program top to bottom
sketch_print_and_strings.bodyMarkdown:
A simple Python program can contain several statements.

For straight-line code like this:

```python
print("First")
print("Second")
print("Third")
```

Python reaches the first statement, then the second, then the third.

The output is therefore:

```text
First
Second
Third
```

The order of the source lines matters.

If you move the last statement to the top:

```python
print("Third")
print("First")
print("Second")
```

the output order changes too.

For now, use this rule for simple programs:

**top source line → next source line → next source line**

Later, conditionals, loops, and functions will make execution paths more interesting. This lesson establishes the basic starting model.

sketch_comments_and_errors.title: Edit, run again, and compare
sketch_comments_and_errors.bodyMarkdown:
Programming is iterative: you rarely write a program once and never touch it again.

A useful loop is:

```text
run → observe → edit → run again → compare
```

Suppose the program is:

```python
print("Status")
print("Version 1")
```

and the new requirement is:

```text
Status
Version 2
```

The first line already does the right thing. A focused edit changes only the second line:

```python
print("Status")
print("Version 2")
```

Then run the program again and compare the new output with the requirement.

This habit matters:

- preserve code that already works
- change the smallest relevant part
- run again
- use the result as feedback

That same loop scales from tiny exercises to larger projects.
